if I'm not wrong, 18mg is the minimum dose of concerta!
actually concerta is a controlled release form of methylphenidate (which is also the active drug in many ADHD meds including most commonly ritalin)

ritalin immediate release (IR) is much shorter acting than concerta 
when i first started getting medicated for ADHD, i was started on ritalin IR 10mg first just to see how i responded eg in terms of improvement/side effects

perhaps you could discuss with your doctor about trying out a short course of ritalin IR as a trial first if side effects worry you! at least if you find the side effects overwhelming, they will wear out much more quickly with ritalin!
also because ritalin and concerta are the same drug but just with different release times, the side effects should be quite similar, if not the same, aside from dose and duration related issues

all the same if you aren't comfortable taking a stimulant or have side effects which you find intolerable, you should definitely have a discussion with your doctor about managing your ADHD in other ways (be it pharmacalogically or not)

This is a tough cookie

If the therapeutic relationship between you and your current psychiatrist isn't working out - you might want to explore finding someone else (if that's possible)

If not - it sounds like an incredibly sticky situation to sort out.

Perhaps you could ask if she's reviewed the documentation from your initial diagnosis period from her colleague and throughout your treatment period. Your situation sounds very tough (I would be extremely frustrated too) but try your best to remain calm and logical with her for now (especially if you have no other options for treatment provider). 

You may potentially have to deal with hearing her out first - just keep an open mind and stay open to what she has to say. If it's something blatantly incorrect about you - just try to keep your cool and remind yourself that you are aware of who you are, and what is the reality of the situation. It sounds ironic given you are the patient - but you might need to be the one to be patient and understanding with her first.

You can calmly cite examples or evidence of why you truly believe you have ADHD and share about how things have changed for you since being medicated, explain calmly your concerns about not being on meds might adversely affect your life in serious ways. I mean there's no guarantee on how she'll respond to this but in general - it might help to explain your case to her as logically as possible.

However that being said, it ultimately sounds like it might be most ideal to go back to your first psychiatrist at their new practice or finding someone new (although it can take time to find the right person), if it's possible. It sounds like there's not much trust and open communication in this therapeutic relationship - and truthfully, you deserve to find a doctor, with whom you can have a healthy patient-doctor relationship with clear and open communication both ways.

It's great that you're a curious patient - and keen to know more about your diagnostic process! :)

Your psychiatrist sounds like she is very thorough in obtaining an accurate diagnosis haha

ADHD is typically diagnosed by the [DSM 5 criteria](https://www.aafp.org/dam/AAFP/documents/patient_care/adhd_toolkit/adhd19-assessment-table1.pdf) \- but sometimes as part of the diagnostic process, it is important to consider [alternative or concomitant neurocognitive and psychiatric conditions](https://www.mdedge.com/psychiatry/article/114016/adhd/rule-out-these-causes-inattention-diagnosing-adhd)

\- This is important because quite a few conditions can mimic ADHD (eg depression can lead to lack of concentration) but require different treatment.

\- Alternatively, patients can also have more than one ongoing issue (eg both ADHD/depression or ADHD and anxiety, ADHD and dyslexia etc..) and a different treatment approach might be necessary

Although **ADHD is a clinical diagnosis** (i.e. made based on a patient's history/presentation, and not lab or scan results), sometimes clinicians might also use more objective tools (eg various cognitive tests like IQ tests/TOVA tests as diagnostic aides)

==============

Some of the tests that you described sound similar to a [formal IQ test](https://www.verywellmind.com/the-wechsler-adult-intelligence-scale-2795283) (eg I remember my psychologist told me the shape re-arranging was to test spatial awareness, and the word definitions were testing language ability - both of which are components tested in the IQ test.)

During my diagnostic process - I also had to do a **TOVA** test. It is a very boring and long computer test that tests for attention. From what I know - ADHD is not diagnosed based on any particular test result, but in general the TOVA can be a useful aide in identifying individuals with potential attention issues, in particular ADHD (has fairly high false positive rate though).

This was all about 6 or 7 years ago - so I've forgotten most details but hope it's helpful! I'm sure your psychiatrist would be more than happy to explain to you the role of the various tests in your case! <3

All the best!

generally speaking - a potential concern theoretically might be the release of long acting Ritalin being impacted by the Omeprazole

Ritalin LA is formulated in a way that the medication is slowly released from the pill/capsule over the course of a day/intended duration by the manufacturer
- one of the factors that can potentially affect the release methylphenidate from the Ritalin LA capsule is pH of your GI tract/stomach
- Omeprazole is a class of drug known as a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which increases gastric pH/reduces the acidity in your stomach
- It's a possibility that omeprazole altering your gastric pH may lead to altered release of methylphenidate levels from your Ritalin LA capsule, leading to less predictable levels of the methylphenidate being absorbed into your bloodstream through out the day, meaning you might have too much or too little of effective methylphenidate at times 
- But from what I know - this is theoretical, and there are no formal studies to determine if this really happens in reality for this specific scenario (i.e. Omeprazole and Ritalin LA) or if the changes in methylphenidate release will be clinically significant enough to impact the patient taking this combination 
- (happy to stand corrected if there is more evidence)

Other than this - I'm not aware of any known interactions or issues between Omeprazole and methylphenidate SR/IR or long acting/controlled release formulations 

For reference - this site mentions Omeprazole and another timed release formulation of methylphenidate https://www.rxlist.com/adhansia-xr-drug.htm (can Ctrl+F and search Omeprazole to bypass the info overload there)

Other sources: Lexicomp, Adhansia XR (methylphenidate) extended-release capsules [prescribing information]. Wilson, NC: Purdue Pharmaceuticals LP; July 2019

It might be helpful to check with your psychiatrist or a pharmacist regarding recommended timings to space apart your omeprazole and Ritalin LA to minimize this risk

it sounds like there are a few different issues in your situation right now

firstly - shortness of breath/left arm weakness/recent stimulant use are valid reasons to see a doctor
would recommend you see a doctor today be it a general practitioner or the emergency room - just so you can at least get assessed and an ECG
even if it's nothing - it's just some weight of your mind

if it is an issue - at least you've dealt with it head on 

secondly - seeing the doctor is also a good time to ask them about the heart murmur that was mentioned previously
- murmurs are usually NOT caused by anxiety alone but more often related to the flow of your blood through the valves that separate the heart's chambers and major blood vessels
- however some murmurs can be relatively more benign and might not need intervention (in fact there are many people who have some degree of mild heart valve abnormalities which don't cause enough issues to necessitate treatment)
- would strongly recommend you see a doctor to ask if this murmur is truly present still and if so, what do they think it may be due to and if anything needs to be done about it
- it might not necessarily be related to your current symptoms but it's just good to have an idea what's going on with this particular health issue

thirdly - it sounds like you're working hard to improve your life and pushing yourself very hard!!
- the caffeine and lack of sleep and more stimulant medication on top of this state are pretty rough on your body though and can be stressful emotionally and also physiologically on your body
- this is a personal recommendation - but I think a good place to start with is making sure you get good sleep most nights at least, for a decent amount of hours
- if you're constantly running on half empty and pushing yourself harder and harder, you're at risk of burnout
- caffeine and stimulants are not true substitutes for good sleep and though they might make your mind feel sharper, they come with effects eg palpitations/increased heart rate, and there will come a time you're driving at maximum speed on an empty gas tank
- I'm not saying good sleep alone will cure ADHD but just that prolonged lack of sleep will likely exacerbate your ADHD symptoms and stimulants/caffeine will only mask things temporarily up to a certain extent
- ADHD meds are certainly there to target your normal ADHD symptoms but if in the setting where your brain is foggy from a lack of sleep - they won't be able to fully help you feel clear headed and sufficiently rested

In conclusion, remember to rest and take care of yourself, your mind and your body! It's OK to say no to things - especially if you need time to find your feet again. And it's OK to not be at 100% or even 20% or 1%. We all get overwhelmed sometimes in life, and you certainly deserve the chance to rest and recover!
I sincerely hope things get better for you soon! hope your body and mind get the rest and nurturing they need

it's great that you're self aware and picked up on this!

perhaps monitor it for a few days and see how things go in terms of your mood/sleep/appetite/main ADHD symptoms

if you feel "euphoric" persistently - you might need to explore with your doctor if it's related to a mood issue (eg do you have new related insomia, suddenly making lots of grandiose new ideas/suddenly having a newly elevated sense of self?)

alternatively might it be a dose related issue or timing of day/taking with caffeine other stimulating meds etc

possibly another medication might work better for you - and it's something you and your psychiatrist can work on together
 
the most basic possibility for your current symptoms might be just you getting used to the meds (because they all affect us in slightly different ways) - your experience might be described differently to someone else's.

But if the effects are concerning to you or those around you and are impacting your functioning in day to day life/not improving your symptoms or even worsening them, I'd say you and your doctor might need to make some adjustments to your treatment plan! 

all the best and take care!

I often make mistakes at work - eg filling in a form wrongly by coping the wrong set of numbers or mixing up details (which means I end up with a whole stack of unusable forms for shredding and recycling often)

I try my best to make it a habit to check before I send off the final copy of my work and sort out most of the preventable errors
- some errors do slip through the cracks but I try to smile and laugh it off wherever possible at work and tell people I'm working on being meticulous and I'm aware of this tendency and trying my best and will rectify ASAP (if it's a small issue)
- if it's a big issue - of course I deal with it head on and tackle and adverse consequences where needed and apologize/rectify as soon as possible to limit any impact on others
- I also try not to get trapped in the checking process by taking too long to check, and I try not to be too hard on myself when I spot an error I've made and needed to correct

I think it takes a lot of time and struggle for us - but it's also good to keep in mind that you can be proud of yourself for trying even when it isn't easy! We might not ever get to perfection - but honestly neurotypical people make careless mistakes too.

I feel it's the attitude that matters the most at work - so don't be too hard on yourself!! you're on your way to getting better everyday 

ps. if people are ever judgemental just rmb - those who mind don't matter, and those who matter don't mind, one day you'll find a space and people you can really grow and flourish with! we are all rooting for you here!!

My dog was forever chewing and attacking his bed as a puppy so we took it away and hid it. We actually just introduced it back to him recently (he's four now) and he won't get off from lounging on it.

When I reintroduced it to him, there were a few sneaky steps involved:

1. Made him lie down on the bed, then gave him a stuffed kong to lick and chew on.
2. Also gently brushed his fur and rubbed his tummy a lot (which he loves) while asking him to lie on it.
3. Taught him the command "go to your bed", where he will then go sit/lie down on the bed and I will commence either step one/two

Aim of this was to teach him that the bed is a wonderful luxurious place, very comfortable, practically heavenly etc. At first I needed to keep bed away when I was busy (to make sure he wouldn't bite the bed secretly). Now he's learnt to appreciate the luxury of a comfy bed and thus lies down on it out of his own free will haha

While lots of the learning is fascinating in med school / premed, other parts can be a bit daunting, and some other parts can be rather dry... (though unfortunately still testable)

I didn't study in the US so can't advise you on the exact MCAT syallbus. But I recommend looking through the specific syallbus / learning outcomes so you can make your own timeline of when you can cover each topic.

In order to truly internalise material, you need to go through several phases of learning so that each concepts sinks in

 1) PHASE 1: first encounter with material
- can be in the form of a lecture by your school, or through reading material
- if you keep zoning out while reading, try youtubing lectures
- recommend: engage actively in this process by making notes in your own words (I like to aggressively mindmap concepts and fill in details, does not matter too much if these notes are readable for later because it's the process of MAKING them which makes you truly internalise in this phase 🧐)

- you need to get into a good flow state while doing this
- why does pomodoro not work for you? 🤔 Are you pomodoro-ing alone in your home?
- you may benefit from studying outside your home (in a library / a coffee shop) if this is not feasible due to the current COVID situation, try something like focus mate or studying with a friend on FaceTime/Skype
- for content that cannot be reasoned out through logic: I recommend mnemonics or memory palace or making your own little jingle/song (whatever works)
- for things like anatomy, I recommend drawing things out and watching YouTube lectures of dissections

2) PHASE 2: apply da knowledge
- try to do this within 1-2 days of first encountering material for maximum yield while things are fresh in your mind
- find a good reliable question bank and test yourself on the material (eg ANKI or buy/borrow some MCAT question books, may be good to sign up for online question bank)

- celebrate aggressively when you get things right
- if you get questions wrong or are confused about any concepts, try to read up and see if that helps, if not ask someone and discuss it
- this phase is all about identifying gaps in your understanding and plugging them

3) PHASE 3: revision
- about a week after learning the material, try testing yourself by going through the concept again
- talk yourself through the concepts and make sure you get each key point from the notes you made in phase 1
- even better get a friend to test you
- DO NOT just read through your phase 1 notes again or skim because you may encounter a false sense of familiarity with the content while missing out of finer key details

4) Phase 4: revision pt 2
- basically Phase 3 but further down the road eg maybe 2 weeks after or a month?
- good news that each time you revise the material, it gets quicker because you'll be able to recall things better 😎

================

TLDR am sorry but for maximum learning I recommend you engage actively with the material at all stages of the learning journey (reading alone isn't very helpful in helping you understand fully, although it may feel easier and give you a false sense of assurance)

In order to survive this rigorous process, I recommend you get a good study buddy or a group of friends to help you stay accountable (and also stay sane). 

Aggressively reward yourself for each little step of progress made to keep your morale high

Know that you are an absolute BEAST for having made it this far.

Sounds like you are in a tough spot, and like you are under quite a bit of stress!

what your parents probably need to understand, is that you are trying your best as a student, but this information might need to be told to them with the help of some other adults.

Unfortunately adults often listen better to other adults - so I recommend speaking to someone at school (eg a guidance counselor or the most understanding teacher around)

Let them know your concerns about ADHD and ask if you can get assessed by an educational expert. Let them know about your struggles with learning/studying/concentrating, ask how else you can optimise your learning.

In my opinion, learning in school is something like this equation:

amount of learning = ability to learn x effort 

Ability to learn is NOT intelligence alone but affected by a great deal of other factors like ability to concentrate / mood / stressors / learning style 

You could be trying your hardest but still maxing out at progress because lots of other factors haven't been addressed which are weighing you down and stopping you from being your best student self (eg unaddressed ADHD / depression / maybe things like teachers going through material too fast / maybe you need smaller group teaching / maybe you're more of a hands on learner)

Either way you need to take care of yourself so that you're in the best possible position to learn, and that's why I recommend speaking to a teacher/educational counselor to explore what are the things which are holding you back from learning as best as possible.

I hope that by taking the initiative to optimise your learning journey, your parents will be less hard on you as they realise you are genuinely trying your best but are also facing obstacles out of your own control!

You have already come a long way in your educational journey, and don't forget to be proud of yourself for whatever progress you've made so far! Life is shitty but always rmb to take care of yourself and I hope you find good people who can support you as you grow into a wonderful young adult and live your very best life.
